article.headline: Ten Films That Think Like Kubrick, Even When They Don't Look Like Him
article.lede: Stanley Kubrick made thirteen features across five decades, which is not very many. The question of what to watch next — once you've exhausted *2001*, *Barry Lyndon*, *The Shining*, and the rest — is genuinely interesting, because the answer isn't genre but sensibility. This list from the account @KubrickPoint attempts exactly that mapping: not films that resemble Kubrick's images, but films that share his preoccupations.
article.body:
The list's organizing logic, unstated but consistent, is that Kubrick was less a genre director than a student of **systems and the people ground up by them**. The Conformist (1970) and There Will Be Blood (2007) sit near each other on that axis — one about a man who joins Italian fascism to dissolve his own terrifying individuality, the other about capitalism as a personality disorder that happens to also drill for oil. Stalker (1979) approaches the same territory from a metaphysical angle: a guide leads two men through a forbidden zone that may or may not grant wishes, and the real subject is the weight of meaning in a world that offers none. All three films treat ideology — political, economic, existential — as a kind of weather that characters move through rather than choose.

Two of the ten entries are by Michael Haneke, and the pairing is instructive. *Funny Games* (1997) is a home-invasion film that periodically stops to address the audience directly, implicating the viewer in their own appetite for screen violence. *Caché* (2005) is slower and more insidious: a bourgeois Parisian couple receives surveillance tapes of their own home, and the film turns guilt — specifically the guilt of comfortable people who prefer not to look — into a formal principle. Haneke's presence here twice is earned; few directors match Kubrick's clinical interest in what watching does to the watcher.

The list is not exclusively about coldness. *Come and See* (1985), Elem Klimov's Soviet war film, is the most viscerally devastating entry — a Belarusian boy's face is the film's entire moral argument, aged by atrocity in real time across two and a half hours. The connection to Kubrick is the point the list makes explicitly: an **unsentimental view of violence**, meaning violence that refuses the comfort of heroism or earned catharsis. *Full Metal Jacket* works the same way. Both films distrust the audience's desire for resolution.

Ingmar Bergman's *Persona* (1966) leads the list and sets the terms. Two women — a nurse and a mute actress — gradually merge identities in a seaside house, while Bergman repeatedly interrupts the film itself: a projector jams, a frame burns, a close-up holds so long the image becomes abstract. The *cinéma vérité* borrowings in *Battle of Algiers* and the hypnotic alienation of Jonathan Glazer's *Under the Skin* (2013) occupy different poles, but both trade in the same Kubrick currency: the camera as an instrument of detachment, watching humans from an uncomfortable distance.

The list's curation is sound. A few entries are canonical recommendations that appear on every art-cinema syllabus (*Persona*, *Stalker*, *Battle of Algiers*), but the inclusion of Seconds (1966) — John Frankenheimer's paranoid nightmare about a man who purchases a new identity and finds it worse than the old one — shows genuine taste. It is the least-seen film on the list and arguably the most Kubrickian in its portrait of modernity as a trap from which style offers no escape.

concepts.definition: A mode of filmmaking defined by long takes, minimal dialogue, and deliberate pacing that prioritizes duration and atmosphere over plot. Tarkovsky is its most celebrated practitioner. The term is descriptive, not pejorative — slowness is the argument, not a failure of editing.

A moment when a film, play, or other fiction directly acknowledges its own artifice or addresses the audience. In Funny Games, a character rewinds the film when a scene goes the wrong way. The device forces viewers to confront their own role in consuming the fiction.

Literally 'cinema truth' in French — a documentary style using handheld cameras, natural light, and non-professional actors to create the texture of lived reality. The Battle of Algiers was shot this way even though it is entirely fictional, and was reportedly mistaken for documentary footage at its release.

A filmmaking stance that refuses to redeem or glamorize on-screen violence through heroism, justice, or emotional catharsis. The violence simply occurs, and the film does not tell the audience how to feel. Kubrick's war films and Come and See are the clearest examples on this list.
